paper_a.title: On asymptotically optimal confidence regions and tests for high-dimensional models

paper_b.title: A significance test for the lasso

metadata.description: Both papers attack post-selection inference for the lasso, but with substantially different theoretical machinery. Paper A (van de Geer-Buhlmann-Ritov-Dezeure) builds the desparsified/debiased lasso via nodewise regression, producing an asymptotically normal pivot $\sqrt{n}(\hat{b}_j-\beta_j^0)$ that yields confidence intervals and tests for individual coordinates uniformly over sparse $\beta^0$. Paper B (Lockhart-Taylor-Tibshirani-Tibshirani) constructs the covariance test statistic $T_k$ along the lasso path and proves an asymptotic $\mathrm{Exp}(1)$ null via discrete-time Gaussian-process / extreme-value arguments. Both target the same problem but the proof techniques (projection / asymptotic linearization vs path-based extreme-value theory) and the inferential targets (individual coefficients vs sequential entry tests) are fundamentally different, making this a competing-frameworks pair.

matches.explanation: Both define the standard lasso estimator as $\ell_1$-penalized least squares (Tibshirani 1996). Both are tagged origin: external. The two formulations differ only by a factor of two and the use of $1/n$ vs $1/2$ scaling, which is purely cosmetic.

Paper A's KKT conditions for the lasso and paper B's lasso fitted-value formula $X\hat{\beta}(\lambda) = P_A y - \lambda(X_A^T)^+ s_A$ are equivalent expressions of the same first-order optimality. Both are external standard convex-analysis facts that the papers use to manipulate $\hat{\beta}$.

Both papers state the central problem of statistical inference for the lasso in high dimensions. Paper A frames it as building asymptotically valid confidence intervals and tests for individual or low-dimensional components of $\beta^0$; paper B frames it as testing $H_0: A \supseteq \mathrm{supp}(\beta^*)$ at each entry along the path. The targets differ (one coordinate at a time vs the variable currently entering the active set), so the match is analogous rather than exact.

These are the central inferential statistics in their respective papers: paper A's desparsified lasso $\hat{b} = \hat{\beta} + \hat{\Theta}\mathbf{X}^T(Y-\mathbf{X}\hat{\beta})/n$ and paper B's covariance test statistic $T_k = (\langle y, X\hat{\beta}(\lambda_{k+1})\rangle - \langle y, X_A\tilde{\beta}_A(\lambda_{k+1})\rangle)/\sigma^2$. Both correct the lasso fit to enable inference, but the constructions are fundamentally different: A subtracts off the bias via an approximate inverse $\hat{\Theta}$ to get a normal pivot for individual coordinates, while B differences full and reduced lasso fits at consecutive knots to build a sequential statistic. They play parallel roles but are mathematically distinct objects.

Paper A's Desparsified-Lasso (Lasso-Pro) procedure computes $\hat{\beta}$, the nodewise relaxed inverse $\hat{\Theta}_{\mathrm{Lasso}}$, and the bias-corrected $\hat{b}_{\mathrm{Lasso}}$ for confidence intervals and tests; paper B's Covariance test procedure runs LARS, computes $T_k$ at each knot, and converts to $p$-values via $\mathrm{Exp}(1)$. Both are the main inferential algorithms of their papers and produce $p$-values / CIs for the lasso, but via incompatible mechanisms (debiasing via nodewise regression vs sequential path-based testing). The composite L2 step alignment is meaningful but the L1-level analogy is the load-bearing one.

Paper A's Theorem 2.2 establishes the asymptotic Gaussian pivot $\sqrt{n}(\hat{b}_{\mathrm{Lasso}} - \beta^0) = W + \Delta$, $W\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_\eps^2\hat\Omega)$, $\|\Delta\|_\infty=o_{\mathbb{P}}(1)$ under random Gaussian design and $s_0 = o(\sqrt{n}/\log p)$. Paper B's Theorems 2 and 3 establish $\mathbb{P}(T_k > t) \to e^{-t}$ (or $\le e^{-t}$) for general $X$ under irrepresentability/conditional-variance/$|S|\gg\log p$ conditions. Both are the main null limiting-distribution theorems for the respective inferential statistic, but with entirely different limit laws (multivariate Gaussian vs Exp(1)) and proof techniques.

Paper A's Corollary 2.1 gives honest (uniform) coverage of the desparsified-lasso CIs over the sparse class $\mathcal{B}(s_0)$. Paper B's Theorem 1 (orthogonal $X$) gives the joint exponential limit $(T_{k_0+1},\ldots,T_{k_0+d})\to(\mathrm{Exp}(1),\mathrm{Exp}(1/2),\ldots,\mathrm{Exp}(1/d))$ under strong-signal orthogonal design. Both are 'clean' orthogonal/random-design results stating the inferential null behavior, but in very different forms (uniform Gaussian CI vs joint exponential).

Paper A's Assumption (A2) is a Gaussian random-design condition with bounded smallest eigenvalue of $\Sigma$ and bounded diagonals. Paper B's Assumptions 2 and 3 are conditional-variance lower bounds plus $|S|\gg\log p$ and irrepresentability. Both are the design-side conditions that make the respective limit theorems go through. They are not equivalent: B's irrepresentability is a strong incoherence requirement that A explicitly avoids, while A's $\Lambda_{\min}$-type bound is replaced in B by a conditional-variance subset condition.

Paper A's fixed-design compatibility assumption (A1) on $\hat\Sigma$ has no counterpart in paper B, which works directly with the design $X$ via projection-based formulas and never invokes a compatibility constant.
Paper A's sub-Gaussian / strongly bounded design conditions (B1)-(B4) extend its results to non-Gaussian errors. Paper B does not study this generalization; its theory is Gaussian-error throughout.
Paper A's GLM high-level conditions (C1)-(C8) drive its convex-loss/M-estimator extension; paper B has no such infrastructure (its GLM/Cox extension is empirical only, captured in CnjP102.1).
Paper A's nodewise weighted-design conditions (D1)-(D5) feed the GLM nodewise theory; paper B has no analogous setup.
Paper A's nodewise-regression lasso (Meinshausen-Buhlmann 2006) is the construction underlying the relaxed inverse $\hat{\Theta}$; paper B never inverts $\hat\Sigma$ and has no analogous estimator.
Paper A's nodewise relaxed inverse $\hat{\Theta}_{\mathrm{Lasso}}$ is the central new object enabling debiasing. Paper B has no analogous matrix; its machinery operates on the lasso path directly.
The extended-KKT bound on $\|\hat\Sigma\hat\Theta_j^T - e_j\|_\infty$ controls how well $\hat\Theta$ inverts $\hat\Sigma$. Paper B never needs such a bound.

The $\ell_1$-penalized M-estimator (GLM lasso) is paper A's GLM building block; paper B's GLM extension stays at the conjecture/simulation level (CnjP102.1) and does not formalize a corresponding object.
Paper A's desparsified GLM estimator has no formal counterpart in paper B, which only conjectures Exp(1) for the GLM/Cox $T_k$ without constructing a new estimator.

Paper A's pivot identity $\hat\beta - \beta^0 + \hat\Theta\lambda\hat\kappa = \hat\Theta\mathbf{X}^T\eps/n - \Delta/\sqrt{n}$ is the algebraic core of the debiasing argument. Paper B has its own pivot decomposition (EP102.2: projection form of $T_k$) but the two are not analogous - they decompose different statistics into different pieces.

Paper A's asymptotic pivot statement $\sqrt{n}(\hat{b}-\beta^0) = W + o_{\mathbb{P}}(1)$ with $W$ Gaussian is the multivariate-normal limit of paper A's procedure; paper B's analogous limit is exponential, so any candidate match would be at the level of TP101.2 vs TP102.2/3 already covered.

Paper A's Theorem 2.1 is the fixed-design representation $\sqrt{n}(\hat{b}-\beta^0) = W + \Delta$ with concentration on $\Delta$. It serves as the building block for TP101.2 (already matched). Treated separately as paper-original with no corresponding fixed-design representation theorem in paper B.
Studentized form of $\hat{b}_{\mathrm{Lasso},j}$. Auxiliary remark; paper B has no analogous Studentization.
Semiparametric efficiency of $\hat{b}_{\mathrm{Lasso},1}$ at the partially linear model is unique to paper A; paper B does not engage with semiparametric information bounds.
Paper A's verification of the semiparametric-efficiency condition in the canonical example has no analogue in paper B.
Nodewise-lasso rates under sub-Gaussian/bounded design are paper A's tool for extending TP101.2 beyond Gaussian errors; paper B has no analogue.
GLM asymptotic-normality theorem (under high-level (C1)-(C8)). No counterpart in paper B.
Nodewise regression with weighted random matrices for the GLM extension. No counterpart in paper B.
Simplified rates corollary for the GLM nodewise estimator. No counterpart in paper B.
Asymptotic-variance lemma for the nodewise estimator (Studentized score $\to\mathcal{N}(0,1)$). No counterpart in paper B's path-based machinery.
GLM asymptotic-normality theorem under primitive conditions. Paper B's conjecture CnjP102.1 covers GLM/Cox at the conjectural level only and is not a proven analogue.
Random-design compatibility-constant lemma for the lasso. Paper B works without compatibility.
Uniform bound on $\max_j 1/\hat\tau_j^2$ for the nodewise lasso. No analogue in paper B.
Consistency lemma $\|\hat\Omega - \Theta\|_\infty = o_{\mathbb{P}}(1)$ for the variance estimate. No analogue in paper B.
Paper A's GLM Lasso-ProG algorithm has no counterpart in paper B.

Proof of TP101.1 via the extended-KKT bound + Lemma 5.1. The proof technique (algebraic decomposition of $\hat{b}-\beta^0$ and pure $\ell_1$/$\ell_\infty$ bounds) has no analogue in paper B's path-based / extreme-value proofs.
Proof of TP101.2 by combining TP101.1 with Lemmas 5.3 and 5.4. The argumentative skeleton is fundamentally different from paper B's tail-control proofs (PP102.7, PP102.11).

Paper A's remaining proofs (Lemmas 5.3, 5.4 and Theorems 2.4, 3.1, 3.3) are all internal to the desparsified-lasso/GLM machinery (concentration, sub-Gaussian rates, linearization of $\dot\rho$) with no counterpart in paper B.

Paper B explicitly defines the linear regression model $y = X\beta^* + \varepsilon$, $\varepsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2 I)$ as a Level-1 paper-origin definition. Paper A also assumes this model but does not encode it as a separate definition node, so there is no L1 counterpart on the A side.
Lasso knots and active set are paper B's core path objects; paper A never decomposes the lasso path into knots.
The reduced lasso $\tilde{\beta}_A$ at the next knot is specific to paper B's covariance-test construction.

Paper B's discrete-time Gaussian processes ($g$, $h$, $g^{(A,s_A)}$) and auxiliary maxima ($M$, $M^+, M^-, M^0$) are the heart of its extreme-value-theoretic proof machinery. Paper A has no analogous Gaussian-process construction.

Strong-signal condition $\min_{j\in A^*}|\beta_j^*| - \sigma\sqrt{2\log p}\to\infty$ is paper B's beta-min for the orthogonal-X case. Paper A explicitly avoids any beta-min assumption (its corollary CP101.1 is uniform over $\mathcal{B}(s_0)$ regardless of signal strength).
Projection form of $T_k$ - internal to paper B's covariance-test algebra.
F-statistic for unknown $\sigma^2$ is paper B's plug-in extension; paper A handles unknown $\sigma_\eps^2$ via the scaled lasso, mentioned only in passing in AP101.1.
Elastic-net covariance statistic is unique to paper B's section 8.1.
GLM/likelihood covariance statistic is paper B's section 8.2 extension; A's GLM theory (TP101.5/3.3) builds a desparsified estimator instead, not a covariance statistic.
Knot form $T_k = C\lambda_k(\lambda_k - \lambda_{k+1})/\sigma^2$ - internal to paper B's representation of $T_k$.
Top-two and joint spacing limits for $\chi_1$ order statistics - paper B's extreme-value-theory ingredients with no counterpart in paper A.
Dual-event representations for the argmax of $g$ - paper B's key probabilistic identity. No analogue in paper A.
Normal-tail-ratio limits used to derive the Exp(1) limit. Internal extreme-value tools of paper B.
Sufficient conditions for $T_1\to\mathrm{Exp}(1)$ and conservative bounds for $\widetilde{T}_k$ / $T_k$ via $M^+$ - the structural lemmas of paper B's tail-control argument. No analogue in paper A.
Variance identity for $g(j,s)$ - internal to paper B's Gaussian-process construction.
Recursion lemma updating $g^{(A,s_A)}$ when one variable is added. No analogue in paper A.

Already partially aligned to CP101.1 under the analogous-orthogonal-result match above; this entry would double-count. Listed here to acknowledge that the orthogonal-X general-step joint exponential limit is a paper-B-original contribution whose closest A-analogue (CP101.1) is matched analogously, not exactly.

Paper B's proofs are uniformly extreme-value / Gaussian-process arguments (Mills ratios, dual-event representations, inductive conditional-variance bounds, EVT theorems of de Haan-Ferreira and Weissman). None of these have analogues in paper A's projection / linearization / nodewise-rate proofs.
